claim: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) account for 10% of the global disease burden.
source: According to WHO, cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) account for 10% of the global disease burden and constitute the number 1 cause of death in the western world.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO data presented in the introduction.

claim: CVDs constitute the number 1 cause of death in the western world.
source: According to WHO, cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) account for 10% of the global disease burden and constitute the number 1 cause of death in the western world.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO data presented in the introduction.

claim: CVDs are mainly caused by behavioral (physical inactivity, unhealthy diet) and metabolic (obesity, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol) risk factors.
source: CVDs are mainly caused by behavioral (physical inactivity, unhealthy diet) and metabolic (obesity, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol) risk factors (Mendis et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mendis et al., 2011.

claim: Aging is by far the biggest contributor to CVD.
source: Aging, however, is by far the biggest contributor to CVD, and aging population is becoming an enormous challenge worldwide.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about aging as a CVD risk factor.

claim: Endothelial cells (ECs) are the most abundant cell population in the adult mouse heart.
source: The heart contains a dense vascular network, and endothelial cells (ECs) are indeed the most abundant cell population in the adult mouse heart (Pinto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pinto et al., 2016.

claim: ECs control vasomotor tone, maintain vascular homeostasis, regulate angiogenesis, and establish bidirectional communication with other cell types and organs via paracrine signaling mechanisms.
source: In addition to their transport function, ECs are defined to control vasomotor tone, maintain vascular homeostasis, regulate angiogenesis, and establish bidirectional communication with other cell types and organs via paracrine signaling mechanisms (Aird, 2007; Aird, 2012; Kivelä et al., 2019; Talman and Kivelä, 2018; Hemanthakumar and Kivelä, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: ECs are highly adaptive to physiological stimuli during normal growth and development.
source: ECs are found to be highly adaptive to physiological stimuli during normal growth and development (White et al., 1998; Bloor, 2005), and the diversity of ECs in different tissues has now been acknowledged.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to White et al., 1998 and Bloor, 2005.

claim: ECs are maladaptive to a spectrum of pathological events involving inflammation or oxidative stress.
source: ECs are also maladaptive to a spectrum of pathological events involving, for example, inflammation or oxidative stress (Cines et al., 1998; Gimbrone and García-Cardeña, 2016), and the development of heart diseases is strongly linked to endothelial dysfunction and impaired vascular remodeling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cines et al., 1998 and Gimbrone and García-Cardeña, 2016.

claim: The development of heart diseases is strongly linked to endothelial dysfunction and impaired vascular remodeling.
source: ECs are also maladaptive to a spectrum of pathological events involving, for example, inflammation or oxidative stress (Cines et al., 1998; Gimbrone and García-Cardeña, 2016), and the development of heart diseases is strongly linked to endothelial dysfunction and impaired vascular remodeling.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Physical inactivity increases the incidence of several chronic diseases.
source: Physical inactivity increases the incidence of several chronic diseases, whereas regular exercise training has positive effects on most of our tissues (Hawley et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hawley et al., 2014.

claim: Regular exercise training has positive effects on most of our tissues.
source: Physical inactivity increases the incidence of several chronic diseases, whereas regular exercise training has positive effects on most of our tissues (Hawley et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hawley et al., 2014.

claim: Exercise trained mice showed improved ejection fraction compared to sedentary mice.
source: Exercise trained mice showed improved ejection fraction compared to the sedentary mice, whereas aging, HFD, and TAC resulted in impaired heart function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Aging, HFD, and TAC resulted in impaired heart function.
source: Exercise trained mice showed improved ejection fraction compared to the sedentary mice, whereas aging, HFD, and TAC resulted in impaired heart function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: HFD induced marked weight gain, increased fat mass, and impaired glucose tolerance.
source: HFD also induced marked weight gain, increased fat mass, and impaired glucose tolerance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: Left ventricular (LV) mass was increased in aged, HFD-treated, and TAC mice.
source: Left ventricular (LV) mass was increased in aged, HFD-treated, and TAC mice (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: Exercise training slightly increased LV mass, which reflects mild physiological hypertrophy often observed in endurance-trained athletes.
source: Exercise training also slightly increased LV mass, which reflects mild physiological hypertrophy often observed in endurance-trained athletes (Arbab-Zadeh et al., 2014; Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Arbab-Zadeh et al., 2014.

claim: Exercise training significantly increased the percentage, count, and mean fluorescence intensity of cardiac ECs compared to controls.
source: Exercise training significantly increased, whereas aging, HFD, and TAC decreased the percentage, count, and mean fluorescence intensity of the cardiac ECs (CD31+CD140a-CD45-Ter119-DAPI-) compared to the controls, when analyzed by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS; Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Aging, HFD, and TAC decreased the percentage, count, and mean fluorescence intensity of cardiac ECs compared to controls.
source: Exercise training significantly increased, whereas aging, HFD, and TAC decreased the percentage, count, and mean fluorescence intensity of the cardiac ECs (CD31+CD140a-CD45-Ter119-DAPI-) compared to the controls, when analyzed by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS; Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Changes in cardiac EC numbers were demonstrated by immunohistochemistry for CD31-positive coronary vessels.
source: This was also demonstrated by immunohistochemistry for CD31-positive coronary vessels (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Isolated cardiac ECs showed significant enrichment of EC markers Cdh5 and Tie1 compared to whole heart or other cardiac mononuclear cells.
source: The cardiac ECs were gated and sorted by FACS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), and the isolated ECs were first analyzed by quantitative PCR analysis, which indicated significant enrichment of EC markers Cdh5 and Tie1 in the sorted fraction compared to whole heart or other cardiac mononuclear cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: EC isolation resulted in 87.4 ± 1.9% cell viability.
source: In addition, isolation resulted in 87.4 ± 1.9% cell viability and RNA purification strategy yielded intact and stable RNA with average RNA integrity number (RIN) of 8.7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: RNA purification strategy yielded intact and stable RNA with average RNA integrity number (RIN) of 8.7.
source: In addition, isolation resulted in 87.4 ± 1.9% cell viability and RNA purification strategy yielded intact and stable RNA with average RNA integrity number (RIN) of 8.7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: Two-dimensional PCA of the EC transcriptomes exhibited significant proportion of variance in the gene expression pattern attributed to treatment-induced changes.
source: Two-dimensional PCA of the EC transcriptomes exhibited significant proportion of variance in the gene expression pattern, which can be attributed to the treatment-induced changes in cardiac EC transcriptome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of EC data sets revealed consistent clustering and high degree of similarity in the gene expression pattern.
source: Notably, unsupervised hierarchical clustering of EC data sets for all experimental interventions (sedentary, exercise trained, young, aged, sham, TAC) revealed consistent clustering and high degree of similarity in the gene expression pattern (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–J.

claim: Exercise training upregulated pathways related to EC development, adherence junction organization, IGFR signaling, adrenomedullin receptor signaling, and mitochondria.
source: The analysis revealed that genes related to EC development, adherence junction organization, IGFR signaling, adrenomedullin receptor signaling, and mitochondria were upregulated by exercise training.
evidence: This claim is supported by PANTHER classification analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Exercise training downregulated pathways related to cellular aging, vascular membrane permeability, negative regulation of angiogenesis, TGF-β1 production, collagen activated tyrosine kinase signaling, and ossification.
source: Furthermore, exercise training downregulated pathways related to cellular aging, vascular membrane permeability, negative regulation of angiogenesis, TGF-β1 production, collagen activated tyrosine kinase signaling, and ossification.
evidence: This claim is supported by PANTHER classification analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Pathways related to TGF-β, IFNα, TNFα, oxidative stress, EC differentiation, vascular permeability, cell aging, collagen synthesis, SMAD signaling, and mesenchymal cell development were highly enriched in cardiac EC from both aged and obese mice.
source: In contrast, pathways related to TGF-β, IFNα, TNFα, oxidative stress, EC differentiation, vascular permeability, cell aging, collagen synthesis, SMAD signaling, and mesenchymal cell development were highly enriched in cardiac EC from both aged and obese mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by PANTHER classification analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Downregulated pathways in aged and obese mice included tissue and lipid homeostasis, ECM assembly, tube morphogenesis, cell adhesion, cell number maintenance, EC proliferation, vasculature development, artery development, and NOTCH signaling.
source: Downregulated pathways in these mice included tissue and lipid homeostasis, ECM assembly, tube morphogenesis, cell adhesion, cell number maintenance, EC proliferation, vasculature development, artery development, and NOTCH signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by PANTHER classification analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Pressure overload activated pathways such as cellular response to TGF-βR2 activation of fibrotic pathways, inactivation of cell survival pathways Erk1/2 and MAPK, and ossification process.
source: Pressure overload activated pathways such as cellular response to TGF-βR2 activation of fibrotic pathways, inactivation of cell survival pathways Erk1/2 and MAPK, and ossification process, whereas cellular homeostasis and vasculature development were repressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by PANTHER classification analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Cellular homeostasis and vasculature development were repressed by pressure overload.
source: Pressure overload activated pathways such as cellular response to TGF-βR2 activation of fibrotic pathways, inactivation of cell survival pathways Erk1/2 and MAPK, and ossification process, whereas cellular homeostasis and vasculature development were repressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by PANTHER classification analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Aging and obesity promoted oxidative stress response, activation of inflammatory and fibrosis pathways, and cellular aging.
source: Aging and HFD promoted oxidative stress response, activation of inflammatory and fibrosis pathways (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E) and cellular aging, and inhibited pathways regulating cell number maintenance, proliferation, and lipid homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Aging and obesity inhibited pathways regulating cell number maintenance, proliferation, and lipid homeostasis.
source: Aging and HFD promoted oxidative stress response, activation of inflammatory and fibrosis pathways (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E) and cellular aging, and inhibited pathways regulating cell number maintenance, proliferation, and lipid homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Exercise training promoted EC homeostasis and vascular growth, and prevented vascular aging, inflammation, and pathological activation.
source: Exercise training, in turn, promoted EC homeostasis and vascular growth, and prevented vascular aging, inflammation, and pathological activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: A significant upregulation of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) genes was observed in cardiac ECs of HFD and TAC-treated mice.
source: In the cardiac ECs of HFD and TAC-treated mice, a significant upregulation of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E) were observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Several clusters of SA-β-galactosidase positive cells were observed in the hearts of HFD-fed mice, which were not observed in chow-fed animals.
source: In HFD-fed mice, we observed several clusters of SA-β-galactosidase positive cells in the heart, which were not observed in the chow-fed animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Quantification showed significant increase in SA-β-galactosidase positive cells in HFD-fed mice.
source: Quantification showed significant increase in these cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Aged and obese mice showed significant upregulation of many mesenchymal markers and downregulation of EC genes.
source: We found significant upregulation of many mesenchymal markers and downregulation of EC genes in aged and obese mice (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: After 2 weeks of TAC, upregulation of several mesenchymal markers was observed.
source: After 2 weeks of TAC, we also observed upregulation of several mesenchymal markers, whereas after 7 weeks of TAC, there was both up- and downregulation of the EC and mesenchymal markers, indicating possible reversal of the process (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: After 7 weeks of TAC, there was both up- and downregulation of the EC and mesenchymal markers, indicating possible reversal of the process.
source: After 2 weeks of TAC, we also observed upregulation of several mesenchymal markers, whereas after 7 weeks of TAC, there was both up- and downregulation of the EC and mesenchymal markers, indicating possible reversal of the process (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F and inference from the pattern of gene expression changes.

claim: Exercise training downregulated several EndMT genes including Fscn1, Cd93, Vwa1, Sparc, Tuba1a, Cd44, Trp53, Col4a2, Mest, Cnn2, Tnfaip1, Lamb1, Ltbp4, and Unc5b.
source: Strikingly, exercise training downregulated several EndMT genes (Fscn1, Cd93, Vwa1, Sparc, Tuba1a, Cd44, Trp53, Col4a2, Mest, Cnn2, Tnfaip1, Lamb1, Ltbp4, and Unc5b), the angiogenesis inhibitor gene Vash1, and the endothelial activation marker Apln and its receptor Aplnr, whereas it upregulated the expression of Malat1, Mgp, Krit1, and Calcrl (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Exercise training downregulated the angiogenesis inhibitor gene Vash1.
source: Strikingly, exercise training downregulated several EndMT genes (Fscn1, Cd93, Vwa1, Sparc, Tuba1a, Cd44, Trp53, Col4a2, Mest, Cnn2, Tnfaip1, Lamb1, Ltbp4, and Unc5b), the angiogenesis inhibitor gene Vash1, and the endothelial activation marker Apln and its receptor Aplnr, whereas it upregulated the expression of Malat1, Mgp, Krit1, and Calcrl (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Exercise training downregulated the endothelial activation marker Apln and its receptor Aplnr.
source: Strikingly, exercise training downregulated several EndMT genes (Fscn1, Cd93, Vwa1, Sparc, Tuba1a, Cd44, Trp53, Col4a2, Mest, Cnn2, Tnfaip1, Lamb1, Ltbp4, and Unc5b), the angiogenesis inhibitor gene Vash1, and the endothelial activation marker Apln and its receptor Aplnr, whereas it upregulated the expression of Malat1, Mgp, Krit1, and Calcrl (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Exercise training upregulated the expression of Malat1, Mgp, Krit1, and Calcrl.
source: Strikingly, exercise training downregulated several EndMT genes (Fscn1, Cd93, Vwa1, Sparc, Tuba1a, Cd44, Trp53, Col4a2, Mest, Cnn2, Tnfaip1, Lamb1, Ltbp4, and Unc5b), the angiogenesis inhibitor gene Vash1, and the endothelial activation marker Apln and its receptor Aplnr, whereas it upregulated the expression of Malat1, Mgp, Krit1, and Calcrl (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Four genes were significantly affected by all treatments (exercise, aging, and HFD): Serpinh1, Vwa1, Mest, and Fhl3.
source: We found four genes significantly affected by all treatments, of which two genes (Serpinh1 and Vwa1) were upregulated by aging and HFD and downregulated by exercise training. The other two genes (Mest and Fhl3) were upregulated by HFD and downregulated by exercise training and aging (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene overlap analysis shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Serpinh1 and Vwa1 were upregulated by aging and HFD and downregulated by exercise training.
source: We found four genes significantly affected by all treatments, of which two genes (Serpinh1 and Vwa1) were upregulated by aging and HFD and downregulated by exercise training.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene overlap analysis shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Mest and Fhl3 were upregulated by HFD and downregulated by exercise training and aging.
source: The other two genes (Mest and Fhl3) were upregulated by HFD and downregulated by exercise training and aging (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene overlap analysis shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Both Serpinh1 and Vwa1 contain a signal peptide for secretion.
source: Both Serpinh1 and Vwa1 contain a signal peptide for secretion, indicating they could act as angiocrines in autocrine and/or paracrine fashion.
evidence: This claim is supported by in silico secretome analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Serpinh1 and Vwa1 could act as angiocrines in autocrine and/or paracrine fashion.
source: Both Serpinh1 and Vwa1 contain a signal peptide for secretion, indicating they could act as angiocrines in autocrine and/or paracrine fashion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the presence of signal peptides.

claim: Serpinh1 has a known role as a collagen chaperone and has been linked to fibrosis.
source: We focused on Serpinh1, as it has a known role as a collagen chaperone and has been linked to fibrosis (Ito and Nagata, 2019), making it an attractive candidate.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ito and Nagata, 2019.

claim: Serpinh1 is expressed in variety of cell types within the mouse heart, including fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, ECs, endocardial cells, and to lesser extent in cardiomyocytes.
source: The scRNAseq analysis revealed that Serpinh1 is expressed in variety of cell types within the mouse heart, including fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, ECs, endocardial cells, and to lesser extent in cardiomyocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: In ECs, Serpinh1 was found to be expressed throughout all EC clusters, with the highest expression in the apelin-high cluster marking activated ECs.
source: In ECs, Serpinh1 was found to be expressed throughout all EC clusters, with the highest expression in the apelin-high cluster marking activated ECs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F.

claim: The expression of mesenchymal markers such as Tagln2, Vim, and Smtn was high in the apelin-high EC cluster.
source: Interestingly, the expression of mesenchymal markers such as Tagln2, Vim, and Smtn was also high in this cluster.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: SERPINH1 is highly expressed throughout the coronary vasculature and in fibroblasts in human heart.
source: Immunohistochemistry demonstrated SERPINH1 to be highly expressed throughout the coronary vasculature and in fibroblasts in human heart, and weak staining was also detected in cardiomyocytes (Figure 4E–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4E–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Weak SERPINH1 staining was detected in cardiomyocytes in human heart.
source: Immunohistochemistry demonstrated SERPINH1 to be highly expressed throughout the coronary vasculature and in fibroblasts in human heart, and weak staining was also detected in cardiomyocytes (Figure 4E–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4E–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In human cardiac ECs, SERPINH1 was localized perinuclearly, consistent with the ER retention motif in its N-terminus.
source: In human cardiac ECs, SERPINH1 was localized perinuclearly, similar to what has been demonstrated in other cells types, and consistent with the ER retention motif in its N-terminus (Figure 4E; Masuda et al., 1994; Razzaque et al., 1998; Honzawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E and citations to previous studies.

claim: The expression of SERPINH1 is highly similar in both veins and arteries and in different tissues.
source: Analysis using the EndoDB database (E-GEOD-43475) showed that the expression of SERPINH1 is highly similar in both veins and arteries and in different tissues (heart, lungs, liver, human cardiac arterial EC (HCAEC), and human umbilical venous EC [HUVEC]) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of publicly available database shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Exercise training can attenuate the expression of Serpinh1 and Vim in aged mice.
source: We next tested, if exercise training can attenuate the expression of Serpinh1, Vwa1, and selected markers of TGF-β signaling/EndMT also in aged mice. Of the studied genes, mRNA expression of Serpinh1 and Vim were significantly repressed by exercise training, and there was a tendency also for Vwa1 (Figure 4H–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H–K.

claim: Overexpression of SERPINH1 altered cellular morphology characterized by impaired or discontinuous vascular endothelial cadherin junctions, increased stress fiber formation, and larger cell size.
source: Overexpression of SERPINH1 altered the cellular morphology characterized by impaired or discontinuous vascular endothelial cadherin junctions, increased stress fiber formation, and larger cell size (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: SERPINH1 overexpression resulted in significant repression of EC markers (CD31, CDH5, TIE1, NRARP, and ID1).
source: Furthermore, analysis of EC and mesenchymal cell-related transcripts demonstrated significant repression of EC markers (CD31, CDH5, TIE1, NRARP, and ID1) and induction of a proliferation gene CCND1, and mesenchymal/EndMT markers (TAGLN, aSMA, CD44, VIM, NOTCH3, ZEB2, SLUG, FN1, VCAM1, and ICAM1) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SERPINH1 overexpression resulted in induction of a proliferation gene CCND1.
source: Furthermore, analysis of EC and mesenchymal cell-related transcripts demonstrated significant repression of EC markers (CD31, CDH5, TIE1, NRARP, and ID1) and induction of a proliferation gene CCND1, and mesenchymal/EndMT markers (TAGLN, aSMA, CD44, VIM, NOTCH3, ZEB2, SLUG, FN1, VCAM1, and ICAM1) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SERPINH1 overexpression resulted in induction of mesenchymal/EndMT markers (TAGLN, aSMA, CD44, VIM, NOTCH3, ZEB2, SLUG, FN1, VCAM1, and ICAM1).
source: Furthermore, analysis of EC and mesenchymal cell-related transcripts demonstrated significant repression of EC markers (CD31, CDH5, TIE1, NRARP, and ID1) and induction of a proliferation gene CCND1, and mesenchymal/EndMT markers (TAGLN, aSMA, CD44, VIM, NOTCH3, ZEB2, SLUG, FN1, VCAM1, and ICAM1) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: VE-cadherin downregulation by SERPINH1 overexpression was confirmed at protein level.
source: VE-cadherin downregulation was also confirmed at protein level (Figure 5D) and increased aSMA expression by immunofluorescence staining (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SERPINH1 overexpression increased aSMA expression.
source: VE-cadherin downregulation was also confirmed at protein level (Figure 5D) and increased aSMA expression by immunofluorescence staining (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SA-β-galactosidase staining showed increased number of cells undergoing senescence in SERPINH1 overexpressing cells.
source: SA-β-galactosidase staining showed increased number of cells undergoing senescence and there was a clear upregulation of senescence-associated genes (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: There was a clear upregulation of senescence-associated genes in SERPINH1 overexpressing cells.
source: SA-β-galactosidase staining showed increased number of cells undergoing senescence and there was a clear upregulation of senescence-associated genes (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: TGF-β1-treatment of HCAECs significantly upregulated the expression of SERPINH1 together with other known EndMT markers.
source: Indeed, our results show that TGF-β1-treatment of HCAECs significantly upregulated the expression of SERPINH1 together with other known EndMT markers, and there was also small but significant induction of SERPINH1 by hydrogen peroxide treatment (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: There was small but significant induction of SERPINH1 by hydrogen peroxide treatment.
source: Indeed, our results show that TGF-β1-treatment of HCAECs significantly upregulated the expression of SERPINH1 together with other known EndMT markers, and there was also small but significant induction of SERPINH1 by hydrogen peroxide treatment (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Four independent shSERPINH1 lentiviral constructs induced approximately 80% deletion of SERPINH1 mRNA.
source: To investigate the significance of SERPINH1 depletion in human cardiac ECs, HCAECs were transduced with four independent shSERPINH1 lentiviral constructs. The constructs induced approximately 80% deletion of SERPINH1 mRNA (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Ten days of SERPINH1 silencing significantly changed EC morphology and decreased the cell density in culture.
source: The cell morphology was not affected after 2 days (Figure 6A), but 10 days of silencing significantly changed EC morphology and decreased the cell density in culture (Figure 6B), suggesting that SERPINH1 might play a role in EC homeostasis and survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: SERPINH1 might play a role in EC homeostasis and survival.
source: The cell morphology was not affected after 2 days (Figure 6A), but 10 days of silencing significantly changed EC morphology and decreased the cell density in culture (Figure 6B), suggesting that SERPINH1 might play a role in EC homeostasis and survival.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed effects of SERPINH1 silencing.

claim: SERPINH1 silencing significantly inhibited collagen fibril deposition.
source: SERPINH1 silencing significantly inhibited collagen fibril deposition, detected by immunohistochemistry for type 1 collagen (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Silencing of SERPINH1 prevented the appearance of Taglin-positive cells induced by TGF-β1 and hydrogen peroxide treatment.
source: The results indicated that silencing of SERPINH1 prevented the appearance of Taglin-positive cells, a commonly used readout for EndMT, which were observed in the control cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Overexpression of SERPINH1 significantly promoted wound closure in scratch wound assay.
source: In the scratch wound assay, overexpression of SERPINH1 significantly promoted wound closure (Figure 7A,B), whereas silencing of SERPINH1 for 2 days significantly decreased EC proliferation/migration (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Silencing of SERPINH1 for 2 days significantly decreased EC proliferation/migration.
source: In the scratch wound assay, overexpression of SERPINH1 significantly promoted wound closure (Figure 7A,B), whereas silencing of SERPINH1 for 2 days significantly decreased EC proliferation/migration (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Cell proliferation was slightly increased by SERPINH1 overexpression.
source: Cell proliferation was slightly increased by SERPINH1 overexpression, whereas silencing almost completely blocked proliferation, as determined by EdU incorporation (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E–G.

claim: SERPINH1 silencing almost completely blocked proliferation.
source: Cell proliferation was slightly increased by SERPINH1 overexpression, whereas silencing almost completely blocked proliferation, as determined by EdU incorporation (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E–G.

claim: CVD risk factors activate transcriptional programs promoting cell aging, senescence, TGF-β activation, inflammation, and oxidative stress in cardiac ECs.
source: The results demonstrate that the CVD risk factors activate transcriptional programs promoting cell aging, senescence, TGF-β activation, inflammation, and oxidative stress in cardiac ECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the overall findings from RNA sequencing and pathway analysis.

claim: Exercise attenuated pathways related to cell aging, senescence, TGF-β activation, inflammation, and oxidative stress, even in healthy mice.
source: Importantly, exercise attenuated these same pathways, even in healthy mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the overall findings from RNA sequencing and pathway analysis.

claim: Aging, obesity, and pressure overload induced mesenchymal gene programs in cardiac ECs.
source: Furthermore, we found that aging, obesity, and pressure overload induced mesenchymal gene programs in cardiac ECs, which can contribute to dysfunctional endothelium and CVD development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the overall findings from RNA sequencing and gene expression analysis.

claim: Mesenchymal gene programs in cardiac ECs can contribute to dysfunctional endothelium and CVD development.
source: Furthermore, we found that aging, obesity, and pressure overload induced mesenchymal gene programs in cardiac ECs, which can contribute to dysfunctional endothelium and CVD development.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed gene expression changes and established knowledge about EndMT.

claim: Serpinh1 was identified as a potential therapeutic target in ECs.
source: SERPINH1 was identified as a potential therapeutic target in ECs.
evidence: This claim is based on the overall findings from the study showing Serpinh1's role in CVD risk factors and EndMT.

claim: SERPINH1 was induced by TGF-β and ROS.
source: Mechanistically, SERPINH1 was induced by TGF-β and ROS, and the overexpression of SERPINH1 increased cell size and stress fiber formation, weakened cell–cell junctions, and promoted mesenchymal and senescence-associated gene expression in human cardiac ECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Overexpression of SERPINH1 increased cell size and stress fiber formation, weakened cell–cell junctions, and promoted mesenchymal and senescence-associated gene expression in human cardiac ECs.
source: Mechanistically, SERPINH1 was induced by TGF-β and ROS, and the overexpression of SERPINH1 increased cell size and stress fiber formation, weakened cell–cell junctions, and promoted mesenchymal and senescence-associated gene expression in human cardiac ECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A-H.

claim: SERPINH1 is abundantly expressed throughout the cardiac vasculature in human hearts.
source: Immunohistochemistry of human hearts showed that SERPINH1 is abundantly expressed throughout the cardiac vasculature.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4E–G.

claim: The largest dysregulation of the cardiac EC transcriptome was found in aged mice, followed by obesity and pressure overload.
source: The largest dysregulation of the cardiac EC transcriptome was found in aged mice, followed by obesity and pressure overload.
evidence: This claim is supported by the number of differentially expressed genes shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: Exercise training affected a smaller number of transcripts compared to CVD risk factors, which can be accounted to the young and healthy control mice.
source: Exercise training affected a smaller number of transcripts, which can be accounted, at least partly, to the young and healthy control mice, which could move unrestrictedly in their home cages.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental design and the number of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Most of the pathways activated by CVD risk factors were the same that were repressed by exercise training.
source: Interestingly, however, most of the pathways activated by CVD risk factors were the same that were repressed by exercise training, highlighting the potential of physical activity to improve cardiovascular health via modulating EC phenotype and function.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The positive effects of exercise on skeletal muscle and cardiac angiogenesis have been described previously.
source: The positive effects of exercise on skeletal muscle and cardiac angiogenesis have been described previously (Hudlicka et al., 1992), but exercise-induced molecular changes in ECs have not been characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hudlicka et al., 1992.

claim: Exercise-induced molecular changes in ECs have not been characterized.
source: The positive effects of exercise on skeletal muscle and cardiac angiogenesis have been described previously (Hudlicka et al., 1992), but exercise-induced molecular changes in ECs have not been characterized.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Regular exercise training promotes stabilization and quiescence in cardiac ECs and prevents cellular aging.
source: This suggests that regular exercise training promotes stabilization and quiescence in cardiac ECs and prevents cellular aging.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed gene expression changes.

claim: Aging and obesity contribute to capillary rarefaction and/or dysfunction.
source: Aging and obesity, on the other hand, are known to contribute to capillary rarefaction and/or dysfunction (Cines et al., 1998; Gimbrone and García-Cardeña, 2016; López-Otín et al., 2013; Ungvari et al., 2010), and another novel aspect in this study was the comparison of several CVD risk factors to identify common pathways and genes, which could drive the pathogenesis in cardiac disease, and could be considered as potential therapeutic targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ECs would provide an attractive target for drug development, as they are the first cells to encounter drugs in the bloodstream.
source: ECs would provide an attractive target for drug development, as they are the first cells to encounter drugs in the bloodstream.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about EC biology and drug delivery.

claim: Dysfunctional endothelium likely contributes to more diseases than any other tissue in the body as it affects all organs.
source: Dysfunctional endothelium likely contributes to more diseases than any other tissue in the body as it affects all organs.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the widespread distribution and functions of endothelium.

claim: Endothelium could act as an important mediator of the health-promoting effects of exercise in a variety of tissues.
source: On the other hand, endothelium could act as an important mediator of the health-promoting effects of exercise in a variety of tissues.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the widespread distribution of ECs and the observed effects of exercise.

claim: Activated endothelial TGF-β signaling and acquisition of mesenchymal features play an important role in the development of EC dysfunction and cardiac diseases.
source: Our finding that aging, obesity, and pressure overload induce mesenchymal gene programs in cardiac ECs adds to the increasing evidence that activated endothelial TGF-β signaling and acquisition of mesenchymal features play an important role in the development of EC dysfunction and cardiac diseases (Kovacic et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2019; Xiong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Genes related to TGF-β production and cellular aging were repressed by exercise.
source: Importantly, genes related to TGF-β production and cellular aging were repressed by exercise, highlighting the potential of exercise training in preventing and delaying the development of CVD.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The molecular mechanisms of exercise-mediated repression of TGF-β signaling are not known.
source: The molecular mechanisms of exercise-mediated repression of TGF-β signaling are not known.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Nitric oxide (NO) has been previously shown to attenuate TGF-β/SMAD2 signaling in ECs.
source: Nitric oxide (NO) has been previously shown to attenuate TGF-β/SMAD2 signaling in ECs, whereas mice lacking endothelial NO synthase activity presented increased TGF-β signaling and collagen 1 in their aortas (Saura et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Saura et al., 2005.

claim: Mice lacking endothelial NO synthase activity presented increased TGF-β signaling and collagen 1 in their aortas.
source: Nitric oxide (NO) has been previously shown to attenuate TGF-β/SMAD2 signaling in ECs, whereas mice lacking endothelial NO synthase activity presented increased TGF-β signaling and collagen 1 in their aortas (Saura et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Saura et al., 2005.

claim: Increased blood flow during exercise induces eNOS expression and NO production, which could repress TGF-β activity in the vasculature.
source: Increased blood flow during exercise induces eNOS expression and NO production, which could repress TGF-β activity in the vasculature.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about exercise physiology and inference from the cited study.

claim: Reduced TGF-β activation was recently reported in whole heart lysates in exercised rats.
source: Reduced TGF-β activation was also recently reported in whole heart lysates in exercised rats (Lin et al., 2020), and enhanced TGF-β signaling was also suggested to be a negative regulator of exercise response in human skeletal muscle (Böhm et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2020.

claim: Enhanced TGF-β signaling was suggested to be a negative regulator of exercise response in human skeletal muscle.
source: Reduced TGF-β activation was also recently reported in whole heart lysates in exercised rats (Lin et al., 2020), and enhanced TGF-β signaling was also suggested to be a negative regulator of exercise response in human skeletal muscle (Böhm et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Böhm et al., 2016.

claim: The activation of TGF-β signaling pathway has been implicated as a driving force for EndMT.
source: The activation of TGF-β signaling pathway has been implicated as a driving force for EndMT (Evrard et al., 2016; Cooley et al., 2014; James and Rafii, 2014; Bischoff, 2019; Bischoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Several studies have recently suggested that EndMT could contribute to the development of various CVDs.
source: Several studies have recently suggested that EndMT could contribute to the development of various CVDs (Zeisberg et al., 2007; Kovacic et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018; Sánchez-Duffhues et al., 2018), but currently there is a lack of understanding of the causal relationships and mechanisms linking EndMT and CVD (Kovacic et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There is a lack of understanding of the causal relationships and mechanisms linking EndMT and CVD.
source: Several studies have recently suggested that EndMT could contribute to the development of various CVDs (Zeisberg et al., 2007; Kovacic et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018; Sánchez-Duffhues et al., 2018), but currently there is a lack of understanding of the causal relationships and mechanisms linking EndMT and CVD (Kovacic et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kovacic et al., 2019.

claim: Whether the transition from ECs to mesenchymal cells occurs completely in various CVDs is still actively debated in the literature.
source: Furthermore, whether the transition from ECs to mesenchymal cells occurs completely in various CVDs is still actively debated in the literature.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Pathological EC activation will result in acquired EndMT features (expression of mesenchymal genes), without full transformation from one cell type to another.
source: It has been suggested that pathological EC activation will result in acquired EndMT features for example expression of mesenchymal genes, without full transformation from one cell type to another (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2020.

claim: All analyzed cells were ECs, but in the CVD risk factor groups they demonstrated increased mesenchymal marker expression.
source: This is in line with our findings, as only cells with high CD31 expression and with no expression of CD45, CD140a, and Ter119 were included in our analyses. Thus, all the analyzed cells were ECs, but in the CVD risk factor groups they demonstrated increased mesenchymal marker expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by the FACS gating strategy and gene expression analysis.

claim: ECs acquire mesenchymal features due to CVD risk factors, which likely results in EC dysfunction even without full EndMT.
source: Our results, however, demonstrate that ECs acquire mesenchymal features due to CVD risk factors, which likely results in EC dysfunction even without full EndMT.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed gene expression changes.

claim: Increased p53 expression in ECs of obese mice has been reported, which led to reduced eNOS phosphorylation both in vitro and in vivo.
source: In ECs of obese mice, increased p53 expression has been reported, which led to reduced eNOS phosphorylation both in vitro and in vivo (Yokoyama et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yokoyama et al., 2014.

claim: Reduced eNOS phosphorylation could result in increased TGF-β activity, linking senescence and TGF-β signaling.
source: Combined with our data, this could then result in increased TGF-β activity (Saura et al., 2005), linking senescence and TGF-β signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited study and the current findings.

claim: Endothelial deletion of p53 has been demonstrated to protect against pressure overload-induced cardiac dysfunction and fibrosis.
source: Endothelial deletion of p53 has also been demonstrated to protect against pressure overload-induced cardiac dysfunction and fibrosis, suggesting that increased p53 and other senescence-associated genes are important mediators of EC dysfunction (Gogiraju et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gogiraju et al., 2015.

claim: Increased p53 and other senescence-associated genes are important mediators of EC dysfunction.
source: Endothelial deletion of p53 has also been demonstrated to protect against pressure overload-induced cardiac dysfunction and fibrosis, suggesting that increased p53 and other senescence-associated genes are important mediators of EC dysfunction (Gogiraju et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited study.

claim: Serpinh1/Hsp47 in myofibroblasts is an important regulator of pathologic cardiac fibrosis.
source: Recently, it was demonstrated using Serpinh1 cell type-specific knockout mice that Serpinh1/Hsp47 in myofibroblasts is an important regulator of pathologic cardiac fibrosis (Khalil et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Khalil et al., 2019.

claim: Collagen 1 production was decreased in EC-specific Serpinh1 deficient hearts in TAC-operated mice.
source: In line with our results, collagen 1 production was decreased also in the EC-specific Serpinh1 deficient hearts in TAC-operated mice (Khalil et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Khalil et al., 2019.

claim: SERPINH1 was found to be important for extracellular collagen 1 deposition and EC proliferation and migration.
source: Furthermore, SERPINH1 was found to be important for extracellular collagen 1 deposition and EC proliferation and migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Silencing of SERPINH1 prevented the TGF-β induced appearance of TAGLIN-positive cells in human cardiac EC.
source: Silencing also prevented the TGF-β induced appearance of TAGLIN-positive cells in human cardiac EC, which is considered as a marker for EndMT (Evrard et al., 2016; Magenta et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and citations to published literature.

claim: TAGLIN-positive cells are considered as a marker for EndMT.
source: Silencing also prevented the TGF-β induced appearance of TAGLIN-positive cells in human cardiac EC, which is considered as a marker for EndMT (Evrard et al., 2016; Magenta et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Evrard et al., 2016 and Magenta et al., 2011.

claim: SERPINH1 is abundantly expressed in all cardiac endothelial populations, as well as in arterial and venous ECs in other tissues.
source: Based on the publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing data and immunohistochemistry of the human heart samples, SERPINH1 is abundantly expressed in all cardiac endothelial populations, as well as in arterial and venous ECs in other tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data and immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements.

claim: SERPINH1 was found to colocalize with several other EndMT markers in some of the ECs in left atrium in patients with atrial fibrillation.
source: In a study by Kato et al., SERPINH1 was found to colocalize with several other EndMT markers in some of the ECs in left atrium in patients with atrial fibrillation, a disease which is often related to fibrosis (Kato et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kato et al., 2017.

claim: Atrial fibrillation is a disease which is often related to fibrosis.
source: In a study by Kato et al., SERPINH1 was found to colocalize with several other EndMT markers in some of the ECs in left atrium in patients with atrial fibrillation, a disease which is often related to fibrosis (Kato et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about atrial fibrillation.

claim: Most of the results represent responses in male mice.
source: In the in vivo experiments for endothelial RNA sequencing analyses, we have used male mice, which were age and gender matched in exercise, obesity, and TAC models. Thus, most of the results represent responses in male mice, whereas in the exercise training experiment in old mice, female mice were used.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental design described in the methods.

claim: Some of the responses, for example the repression of Serpinh1 in exercised mice, were similar in old female mice to those observed in young male mice.
source: Some of the responses, for example the repression of Serpinh1 in exercised mice, were similar to those observed in young male mice; however, some of the changes were not significant in old female mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H-K.

claim: Some of the changes were not significant in old female mice.
source: Some of the responses, for example the repression of Serpinh1 in exercised mice, were similar to those observed in young male mice; however, some of the changes were not significant in old female mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H-K.

claim: CVD risk factors significantly remodel the cardiac EC transcriptome promoting cell senescence, oxidative stress, TGF-β signaling, and mesenchymal gene features.
source: In conclusion, our data demonstrate that the major CVD risk factors significantly remodel the cardiac EC transcriptome promoting cell senescence, oxidative stress, TGF-β signaling, and mesenchymal gene features, whereas exercise training provided opposite and protective effects (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by the overall findings from the study and summarized in Figure 8.

claim: SERPINH1 was identified as one of the downstream effectors of TGF-β, which could provide a novel therapeutic target in ECs.
